The appellant is wrong to suggest that a relevant distinction can be drawn between the facts of
Mainpay
and those of this case with the result that, unlike in
Mainpay
, HMRC have to prove a particular counter-factual outcome. The CA’s reasoning in
Mainpay
CA

was not based on the degree of complexity in the issue of law that arose in that case. In any event, as HMRC have consistently maintained, resolution of the issue in this case was straightforward in light of
Grays Timber

content.p: In the alternative, even if HMRC are required to make out a prima facie case as to what would have happened but for the carelessness, HMRC have shown, prima facie, that there would then have been no loss of tax: (a) but for the carelessness, Mr Ricupati would have obtained specialist employment tax advice, (b) he would have requested relevant information from the sellers and/or EY Sauflon before seeking that advice and would have provided all relevant information to the adviser, and/or raised further questions of EY Sauflon and set out the information received, (c) accordingly, he would have obtained Mr Kilshaw’s email in which he stated that the price differential was “aggressive”, (d) it would have been apparent that Mr Wells held such a dominant position that he was able to dictate that he did not wish to pay tax on his sale proceeds and, when he was advised that the original structure of the transaction involving “forward-looking warranties” would not achieve that aim, to secure a change in the structure with the adoption of two agreements, (e) it would have been apparent that the two agreements structure was adopted specifically to give the impression that there had been separate negotiations when it was known that was not the case, (f) it would have been apparent that a number of special circumstances influenced the allocation of the consideration between the shareholders: (i) Mr Wells’s dominant position included the ability to “blow up the deal”, (ii) Prism, by contrast, was eager to sell its stake in the appellant, (iii) as part of the agreement on allocation, Mr Maynard and Mr Wells had agreed to discontinue legal proceedings against Prism, (iv) part of the price received by Mr Wells and Mr Maynard for their shares represented a reward for work that they had done, and (g) it would have been clear to the adviser from appendix 1 of the memo that EY Sauflon’s advice was based on a misstatement of the factual position.

p.span: HMRC have made out a prima facie case that, on the balance of probabilities, the adviser would have advised, on the basis of all the relevant information, including that set out above, that the price actually received by the shareholders did not represent market value, and that income tax and NICs were payable on the excess over their pro-rata share of the consideration pursuant to the applicable statutory provisions. HMRC essentially repeated their submissions as regards the market value test. They added that the fact that the transaction was structured in an attempt to reduce the tax liability of Mr Wells in particular, by way of the features identified above, and that EY Sauflon’s advice was based on a misstatement of the factual position, (as revealed by appendix 1 of the memo) would have made the adviser more inclined to question whether the allocation of the consideration between the selling shareholders reflected the market value of their respective shares. Further and in any event, the adviser would have concluded that the amounts actually received by the shareholders for their shares did not represent the market value” for the purposes of guidelines to which Mr Weaver referred.

intro.p: In written submissions the appellant made the following main points in support of their stance that any carelessness did not cause any loss of tax:

content.p: As regards what HMRC is required to prove, it is notable that in Mainpay the taxpayer argued that it was “necessary for HMRC to establish with precision the “counter-factual” situation in order to prove causation” (see Mainpay UT at [147(1)] and Mainpay CA at [84]) and that HMRC had “failed to explain at all or in sufficient detail”:

p.span: What was it that HMRC were alleging Mainpay should actually have done or known?
When is it said that Mainpay should have done or known that?
Why is it said that Mainpay should have done or known that?
If Mainpay had done or known the thing in question, how would matters have been any different in relation to the loss of tax?” (see
Mainpay UT

content.p: That is what the CA referred to (using the words of the UT in Mainpay UT) as “a particular counter-factual outcome”. The CA held that the burden of proof on HMRC does not extend to them having to prove all of those particulars. Thus, for example, HMRC do not have to go as far as to prove what, in the counterfactual scenario, the taxpayer’s subsequent response to consulting an appropriate advisor would have been (see Mainpay CA at [117]).

Hence, what HMRC are required to prove by way of satisfying the causation requirement will differ depending on the facts and the nature of the conduct which HMRC allege was careless. The fact-sensitive nature of the causation analysis is referred to throughout the judgment. That is because the hypothetical scenario that must be examined in order to test causation depends on the particular facts.

In this context, there is a difference between a failure to consult a lawyer in relation to a particular form of contract, which any competent lawyer could produce if asked to do so (as in Mainpay), and a failure to obtain a (further or other) opinion on a complex issue of valuation in respect of which reasonable minds can differ (as here). HMRC allege that any reasonable and prudent taxpayer in the position of the appellant would have taken further or other advice on the issue. To establish that careless conduct of that nature caused the relevant loss of tax, HMRC must prove that: “Had [the taxpayer] taken reasonable care [i.e. taken further or other advice] … that loss of tax would have been avoided” (see Mainpay CA at [116]).

However, HMRC have not proved that (a) even if further advice had been sought from EY Sauflon, the advice would have been any different to the advice actually given, and/or (b) that a different advisor would have given any different advice. There is no feasible argument that, if such advice had been sought, any competent advisor would have advised in a different way. For example, EY and LW can be taken to have been aware of Grays Timber (as it is a Supreme Court case from 2010); it (rightly) had no bearing on their advice. Moreover, Mr Weaver’s valuation opinion, based on the facts and evidence in this case, is essentially the same as the valuation opinion given by EY Sauflon in 2014. Accordingly, the only evidence before the tribunal on the point is that another advisor would have advised in the same way as EY Sauflon did.

Mainpay CA has established that, for the carelessness test in s 36 TMA to be satisfied, HMRC must make a prima facie case (on the balance of probabilities) that (1) the appellant failed to take reasonable care as regards the tax charges in question (as for all the reasons set out above we consider they have) and (2) that that failure to take reasonable care caused the relevant loss of tax. As the appellant emphasised, it is apparent that precisely what HMRC must prove as their prima facie case, to satisfy this causation requirement, will differ depending on the facts and the nature of the conduct which HMRC allege was careless. HMRC may not necessarily have to prove all the particulars of a counter factual or hypothetical outcome. The parties’ differing views of what HMRC are required to prove in this case reflects their differing views of how the market value test is to be applied and of the factual conclusions to be made on the PAYE issue.

In our view, in light of our findings on the PAYE issue set out above, on the facts of this case, HMRC have made a prima facie case that the appellant’s failure to account for income tax and NICs in respect of the price differential was brought about by the appellant’s/Mr Ricupati’s failure to take reasonable care. As set out in our conclusions above, we consider that, in all the circumstances, a reasonable taxpayer would have sought its own specialist advice on the PAYE issue from a suitably qualified professional adviser, on providing the adviser with all relevant information known to the taxpayer regarding the negotiations on (a) the price for all the shares in the appellant between CV and Mr Wells, and (b) on the allocation of that price between the selling shareholders. We recognise that the appellant itself obtained advice from EY Sauflon. However, Mr Ricupati/CV did not know the basis on which the advice was provided, as they were not privy to the instructions and information given to EY Sauflon, given that, when the advice was given, the appellant was in the ownership of the sellers. Moreover, for all the reasons set out above, a reasonable taxpayer would have conducted a critical scrutiny of the memo and valuation letter and, in doing so, would have realised from their terms that there was cause for concern that the advice in the memo and valuation letter was not reliable.

In our view, the view of the market value test taken by the appellant is not one which any reasonable suitably qualified professional adviser would take. In light of the case law on how the market value test is to be applied, in particular, the decision in Grays Timber, which any such adviser can be taken to be aware of, and of the factual position, as known to Mr Ricupati/the appellant, (1) we can see no viable basis for such an adviser, apprised of those facts, to take the view that the best evidence of what the hypothetical seller and buyer envisaged in the market value test would agree for the shares is the agreed allocation of the total price for the shares negotiated between the selling shareholders, and (2) it is reasonable to infer that, had Mr Ricupati consulted such an adviser on that basis, he would have advised that (a) the best evidence of market value of the shares for this purpose is the price paid by CV for the shares on a pro rata basis, and (b) accordingly, the appellant should account for income tax and NICs in respect of the price differential.

As set out in our conclusions above, we consider that a reasonable taxpayer also would have asked EY Sauflon/the selling shareholders for further information on their negotiations and precisely what instructions and information they had provided to EY Sauflon. However, we do not consider it is necessary or appropriate to speculate as to what information EY Sauflon/the selling shareholders may or may not have provided in response. In our view, (1) a reasonable taxpayer in any event would have sought its own specialist advice in these circumstances for the reasons summarised in [294], and (2) the matters which were within Mr Ricupati’s/CV’s own knowledge (as highlighted in our conclusions on the carelessness issue above), which a reasonable taxpayer would have informed its adviser of, would have sufficed to alert any such adviser to the fact that there is no reasonable basis for the opinion given in the memo/valuation letter and to inform the correct view.

On that basis, if the appellant wishes to contradict the prima facie case made by HMRC, there is an evidential burden on the appellant to bring evidence to show that (on the balance of probabilities) it/Mr Ricupati did not fail to take reasonable care or that any such failure did not bring about the loss of tax in this case. The appellant has not done so.

p.span: Conclusion and right to appeal

content.p: For all the reasons set out above the appeal is dismissed except so far as it relates to the consideration received by the shareholders for the Fourth Shares.

This document contains full findings of fact and reasons for the decision. Any party dissatisfied with this decision has a right to apply for permission to appeal against it pursuant to Rule 39 of the Tribunal Procedure (First-tier Tribunal) (Tax Chamber) Rules 2009. The application must be received by this Tribunal not later than 56 days after this decision is sent to that party. The parties are referred to “Guidance to accompany a Decision from the First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber)” which accompanies and forms part of this decision notice.
RELEASE DATE: 02nd MARCH 2026

p.span: APPENDIX
Decision on expert evidence
DECISION ON ADMISSIBILITY OF EXPERT EVIDENCE
Overview

blockContainer.p: The relevant background is as follows:
On 5 May 2022, the appellant gave notice that it intended to rely upon expert valuation evidence in relation to the market value of the shares.
On 26 October 2023, the appellant served on HMRC Mr Weaver’s expert report.
On 22 November 2023, HMRC informed the appellant that they intend to rely on expert evidence in reply to the report and that their evidence would be served by 23 February 2024.

On 26 January 2024, HMRC stated that their view was that expert evidence would be “usurping the function of the Tribunal”. On 28 October 2024 HMRC indicated in their skeleton argument that they would make an application to exclude Mr Weaver’s report from being admitted as evidence in these proceedings.

On 15 November 2024, HMRC made their application during the hearing of this appeal. It was agreed that the application would be dealt with after the hearing on the basis of the parties’ written submissions and the tribunal would hear evidence from Mr Weaver at the hearing.

Rule 2(1) of the Tribunal Procedure (First-tier Tribunal) (Tax Chamber) Rules 2009 (“the Rules”) provides that: “The overriding objective of these Rules is to enable the Tribunal to deal with cases fairly and justly”. Rule 2(3) provides that the tribunal “must seek to give effect to the overriding objective when it - (a) exercises any power under these Rules; or (b) interprets any rule or practice direction”.
Rule 5(1) and (2) of the Rules provide as follows:

p.span: Subject to the provisions of the 2007 Act and any other enactment, the Tribunal may regulate its own procedure.
The Tribunal may give a direction in relation to the conduct or disposal of proceedings at any time, including a direction amending, suspending or setting aside an earlier direction.”

blockContainer.p: Rule 15 of the Rules provides as follows:

p.span: - (1) Without restriction on the general powers in rule 5(1) and (2) (case management powers), the Tribunal may give directions as to -
issues on which it requires evidence or submissions;
the nature of the evidence or submissions it requires;
whether the parties are permitted or required to provide expert evidence, and if so whether the parties must jointly appoint a single expert to provide such evidence;
The Tribunal may -
admit evidence whether or not the evidence would be admissible in a civil trial in the United Kingdom; or
exclude evidence that would otherwise be admissible where -
the evidence was not provided within the time allowed by a direction or a practice direction;
the evidence was otherwise provided in a manner that did not comply with a direction or a practice direction; or
it would otherwise be unfair to admit the evidence.”

blockContainer.p: HMRC submitted that:

The tribunal should exclude Mr Weaver’s evidence on the basis that it is not reasonably required to resolve the market value issue. That is on the basis that the tribunal should follow the position set out in the Civil Procedure Rules (specifically rule 35.1) that expert evidence shall be restricted “to that which is reasonably required to resolve proceedings”. The shares in question in this case were in fact sold on the valuation date. The tribunal’s task is to decide whether the market value of the shares was (a) the total consideration paid by the purchaser divided by the number of shares, or (b) the price received by the shareholders according to the division of sale proceeds said to have been agreed with the other shareholders. In those circumstances, the expert evidence is not reasonably required by the tribunal to answer the statutory question.

Further or alternatively, Mr Weaver’s evidence should be excluded because it usurps the tribunal’s function. It sets out to answer the very question that the tribunal must answer in relation to market value. It purports to make extensive findings of fact, going beyond mere assumptions, and it does so based on an incomplete view of untested evidence. It then applies the relevant statutory provision, read with valuation standards that simply reflect the relevant case-law principles, to the facts as found.

p.span: Mr Weaver’s expert report and oral evidence

blockContainer.p: Mr Weaver is a chartered accountant of over 30 years’ valuation and advisory experience and a managing director in the valuations advisory services practice at Kroll. His area of expertise is in the valuation of all types of financial assets for a variety of reasons, including tax and financial reporting. In his report he concluded that the shareholders’ shares in the appellant were not disposed of for an amount which exceeded the market value of those shares at the time of their disposal.

He referred to the International Valuation Standards (“IVS”) issued by the International Valuation Standards Council, which he said was the key guide for valuation professionals globally to underpin consistency, transparency and confidence in valuations. He relied, in particular, on para 30 of IVS 104 (Bases of Value):

p.span: “30.1. Market Value is the estimated amount for which an asset or liability should exchange

on the valuation date between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s length transaction, after proper marketing and where the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently and without compulsion
30.2. The definition of Market Value shall be applied in accordance with the following conceptual framework:
(a) “the estimated amount” refers to

a price expressed in terms of money payable for the asset in an arm’s length market transaction. Market Value is the most probable price reasonably obtainable in the market on the valuation date in keeping with the market value definition. It is the best price reasonably obtainable by the seller and the most advantageous price reasonably obtainable by the buyer

. This estimate specifically excludes an estimated price inflated or deflated by special terms or circumstances such as atypical financing, sale and leaseback arrangements, special considerations or concessions granted by anyone associated with the sale, or any element of value available only to a specific owner or purchaser….

(b) “an asset or liability should exchange” refers to the fact that the value of an asset or liability is an estimated amount rather than a predetermined amount or actual sale price. It is the price in a transaction that meets all the elements of the Market Value definition at the valuation date,
(c) “on the valuation date” requires that the value is time-specific as of a given date….,

between a willing buyer” refers to one who is motivated, but not compelled to buy. This buyer is neither over eager nor determined to buy at any price. This buyer is also one who purchases in accordance with the realities of the current market and with current market expectations,

rather than in relation to an imaginary or hypothetical market that cannot be demonstrated or anticipated to exist. The assumed buyer would not pay a higher price than the market requires. The present owner is included among those who constitute “the market”,

and a willing seller” is neither an overeager nor a forced seller prepared to sell at any price, nor one prepared to hold out for a price not considered reasonable in the current market. The willing seller is motivated to sell the asset at market terms for the best price attainable in the open market after proper marketing, whatever that price may be.
The factual circumstances of the actual owner are not a part of this consideration because the willing seller is a hypothetical owner,

(f) “in an arm’s length transaction” is one between parties who do not have a particular or special relationship….The Market Value transaction is presumed to be between unrelated parties, each acting independently,

(g) “after proper marketing” means that the asset would be exposed to the market in the most appropriate manner to effect its disposal at the best price reasonably obtainable in accordance with the market value definition. The method of sale is deemed to be that most appropriate to obtain the best price in the market to which the seller has access. The length of exposure time is not a fixed period but will vary according to the type of asset and market conditions. The only criterion is that there must have been sufficient time to allow the asset to be brought to the attention of an adequate number of market participants. The exposure period occurs prior to the valuation date,

(h) “where the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently” presumes that both the willing buyer and the willing seller are reasonably informed about the nature and characteristics of the asset, its actual and potential uses, and the state of the market as of the valuation date. Each is further presumed to use that knowledge prudently to seek the price that is most favourable for their respective positions in the transaction. Prudence is assessed by referring to the state of the market at the valuation date, not with the benefit of hindsight at some later date. For example, it is not necessarily imprudent for a seller to sell assets in a market with falling prices at a price that is lower than previous market levels. In such cases, as is true for other exchanges in markets with changing prices, the prudent buyer or seller will act in accordance with the best market information available at the time,
(i) “and without compulsion” establishes that each party is motivated to undertake the transaction, but neither is forced or unduly coerced to complete it.” (Emphasis added.)

blockContainer.p: He also referred to guidance given in para 20 of IVS 105 (Valuation Approaches and Methods) as providing guidance on the approach which is commonly used by valuers:

p.span: “The market approach provides an indication of value by comparing the asset with identical or comparable (that is similar) assets for which price information is available.
20.2. The market approach should be applied and afforded significant weight under the following circumstances:
(a) the subject asset has recently been sold in a transaction appropriate for consideration under the basis of value,
(b) the subject asset or substantially similar assets are actively publicly traded, and/or
(c) there are frequent and/or recent observable transactions in substantially similar assets.

20.3. Although the above circumstances would indicate that the market approach should be applied and afforded significant weight, when the above criteria are not met, the following are additional circumstances where the market approach may be applied and afforded significant weight. When using the market approach under the following circumstances, a valuer should consider whether any other approaches can be applied and weighted to corroborate the value indication from the market approach:
(a) Transactions involving the subject asset or substantially similar assets are not recent enough considering the levels of volatility and activity in the market.
(b) The asset or substantially similar assets are publicly traded, but not actively
(c) Information on market transactions is available, but the comparable assets have significant differences to the subject asset, potentially requiring subjective adjustments.
(d) Information on recent transactions is not reliable (ie, hearsay, missing information, synergistic purchaser, not arm’s-length, distressed sale, etc).
(e) The critical element affecting the value of the asset is the price it would achieve in the market rather than the cost of reproduction or its income-producing ability.

20.4. The heterogeneous nature of many assets means that it is often not possible to find market evidence of transactions involving identical or similar assets. Even in circumstances where the market approach is not used, the use of market-based inputs should be maximised in the application of other approaches (e.g., market-based valuation metrics such as effective yields and rates of return).

20.5. When comparable market information does not relate to the exact or substantially the same asset, the valuer must perform a comparative analysis of qualitative and quantitative similarities and differences between the comparable assets and the subject asset. It will often be necessary to make adjustments based on this comparative analysis. Those adjustments must be reasonable and valuers must document the reasons for the adjustments and how they were quantified.

20.6. The market approach often uses market multiples derived from a set of comparables, each with different multiples. The selection of the appropriate multiple within the range requires judgement, considering qualitative and quantitative factors.”

blockContainer.p: Mr Weaver made the following main points in his report:

As a valuer tries to simulate a hypothetical market transaction, the first step is to consider any recent actual transactions in the subject asset or business, as the price paid in an actual transaction carried out in a market with similar characteristics to the hypothetical transaction represents the best evidence of market value. This is supported by:
Para 20 set out above.
The International Private Equity and Venture Capital Valuation Guidelines of December 2022 (“Guidelines”) which discuss the concept of fair value as defined as:

p.span: “1.1 Fair Value is the price that would be received to sell an asset in an Orderly Transaction between Market Participants at the Measurement Date…Fair Value is the hypothetical exchange price taking into account current market conditions for buying and selling assets. Fair Value is not the amount that an entity would receive or pay in a Forced Transaction, involuntary liquidation, or distressed sale.”

blockContainer.p: The relevant comment he relied on is:

p.span: “The Price of a Recent Investment, if resulting from an orderly transaction, generally represents Fair Value as of the transaction date.”

blockContainer.p: We refer to this concept as a “recent price”.

The Shares and Assets Valuation Manual published by HMRC under the reference SVM113110 which is commonly used as a reference by valuers for tax purposes, states that the evidence of prior and similar transactions are considered to be helpful evidence of market value.

If a transaction has occurred exactly on the valuation date on arm’s length terms, between willing parties who were under no compulsion to sell, for a shareholding with identical rights as the subject shareholding, it is standard valuation practice for a valuer to use this price as the best estimate of the market value of the subject shareholding.

He had considered the market value of the shareholders’ combined shares in the context of the actual demand in the real-world market, where all the other shareholdings in the appellant were also available for sale, and what the highest bidder would have offered. In this context he stated that (a) the shareholders negotiated as an alliance (through Mr Maynard as their representative) with the other two sellers’ groups, (b) the actual demand at the relevant time (on 6 August 2014) was for 100% of the shares in the appellant, and (c) the transaction was the product of three separate negotiations, between (i) the shareholders and the minority shareholders, (ii) the shareholders and CV, and (iii) the shareholders and the other majority shareholders.

He considered that the relevant criteria are satisfied for fair market value to be taken to be the recent price as agreed in relation to the transaction if (a) all the negotiating groups involved were unrelated willing parties, acting in their own economic best interests, (b) none of the selling shareholders were under any compulsion to sell their shares, (c) the market conditions, as at the transaction date, were the same as those as at the valuation date (6 August 2014), and (d) the transaction took place in the open market.
In considering this he noted the following:

On the sale of their shares (i) Prism received £1,539.08 per share for each of their A ordinary and ordinary shares and Bond received £1,555.14 for each preference share, (ii) the rights attaching to the ordinary shares were almost identical but the preference shares had preferential rights over a certain percentage of profit after tax before any distribution to the ordinary shareholders, (iii) both minority shareholders willingly agreed to accept the prices offered, (iv) the outcome of this negotiation seems reasonable based on Mr Maynard’s report that Prism had already tried to sell their shares to “another private equity company…” and the price they were then looking for, (v) the appellant’s articles contained provisions which meant that if any of the other majority shareholders ceased to be an employee, their shares would be immediately sold back to the company at fair value (as defined in the Articles), and the negotiations with those persons resulted in them accepting the proceeds and price per share offered by Mr Maynard for their stakes, (vi) there were separate negotiations with CV, (vii) all parties were acting in a commercial manner, and (viii) in his experience it is fairly common for private equity investors to have contractual terms similar to those attaching to the preference shares, and also to have rights that enable them to force a sale of the company but there were no such rights.

(i) Based on the way the negotiations were conducted and the differing rights attaching to the shares involved in each negotiation, it is reasonable to consider these three sets of negotiations as separate, as further supported by the different share sale and purchase agreements and deeds, and (ii) as the shareholders acted as an alliance in completely separate discussions, “they were able to agree a price that would be accepted for the shareholdings of the [minority shareholders] and the [other majority shareholders] and negotiate and sell 100% of the shares in the [appellant] to [CV]”.

The shareholders owned a majority stake in the appellant and the price at which they were willing to sell their stake was higher than the other shareholders, as evidenced by their reactions to the multiple approaches by various trade buyers. Mr Wells had previously walked away from a potential sale of the business in 2012 in the final stage of negotiations, which was known to all shareholders.

Prism tried to sell their shares in the appellant to “another private equity company…” for £41 million to £55 million and Mr Maynard said that Prism wished to close its fund. That evidences the price which Prism were willing to accept as a willing seller in a sale of their minority shareholding on its own. Prism were motivated to sell their shares in the appellant, but there is nothing to suggest they were compelled to sell their shares as part of the transaction. The fact that negotiations with Prism were “difficult” supports that Prism engaged in arm’s length negotiations to try to get the best deal for themselves, in terms of the best price for their stake achieved through a combination of Mr Wells’ negotiations with CV and their negotiations with Mr Maynard.

Bond, whilst not as motivated to sell as Prism, may have recognised that Mr Wells and Mr Maynard “were not getting any younger, and they wanted to cash in their money at some stage and thought that this was probably a good time to do so”, in 2014 when the offer from CV was under negotiation. Nothing suggests that Bond were compelled to sell their shares as part of the transaction. There is evidence they did try to negotiate for a higher price compared with Prism as they thought that they had been more supportive.

The minority shareholders had a relatively weak negotiating position due to (i) the shareholders having a majority shareholding in the appellant and being less motivated to sell, and (ii) the minority not having any contractual terms that allowed them to force the shareholders to sell their shares. It can be presumed that they acted in a rational manner in their own economic best interests, and willingly accepted the price that was offered, based on their significantly weaker negotiating position. Prism received £149.4 million for their stake and Mr Maynard’s statement that “Prism were happy with the deal they obtained, as shown by the press report from Private Equity News” is consistent with the presumption that Prism was a willing but not an overeager seller.

Based on the above, he concluded that (a) Prism was a willing seller who accepted the price for their shares that they ultimately received and were satisfied that it was the highest that they could have reasonably achieved for their shares considering their rights, (b) that price was significantly more than they would have received if they had sold their shares separately to a third party, as private equity companies seek to maximise value and can therefore be expected to have explored all possible avenues for sale, (c) the fact that they chose to sell their shareholding implies that they considered this was the best price that they could achieve for their shares, (d) as their non-controlling stake did not give them the power to force the shareholders to sell their shares, and given the shareholders’ negotiating position, effectively they had to persuade the shareholders to sell their controlling stake as part of the transaction, which meant them accepting proceeds that were lower than the prices per share received by the other shareholders, and (e) therefore, as they were willing sellers, the proceeds and price per share accepted by them represents market value for their respective minority stakes in the appellant.

As regards negotiations with CV: (a) this was an arm’s length negotiation between unrelated parties, with CV acting in their own economic best interests and Mr Wells acting in the economic best interests of the selling shareholders to ensure that they collectively received the highest possible price for the appellant, (b) CV was one of the three trade buyers (out of the four main companies in the contact lens industry) who expressed interest in acquiring the appellant during the years 2011 to 2014, all of whom could be expected to gain some synergistic benefits from acquiring the appellant, (c) since CV was to acquire 100% of the appellant, CV was likely to have had access to the usual level of information available with respect to the present position of the business and its future prospects, (d) CV conducted negotiations for almost six months before completing the acquisition, which is a normal timeframe for an acquisition process, and (e) CV had engaged advisors to assist them on the acquisition. That indicates it acted as a prudent buyer. He considered that the highest price a prudent purchaser would pay for 100% of the shares in the appellant is the price paid by CV as part of the transaction.

As regards the negotiation with the other majority shareholders: (a) the others were initially unhappy with the price offered but Mr Maynard, acting on behalf of the shareholders, emphasised their minority position and that this was “the price they were going to have to accept for their shares”, (b) he states that if they did not sell their shares as part of an overall sale of the appellant, they would not have been able to realise the value of their shares, and (c) these shareholders were also subject to additional provisions whereby they were forced to sell their shares at fair value if they were no longer employed. He considers this supports a presumption that the other shareholders engaged in arm’s length negotiations to try to get the best deal for themselves. There is no evidence to suggest that they were related to each other or to any of the other parties involved in the transaction, or that they were under any compulsion to sell their shares at that time or as part of the transaction. Therefore, he presumes that they acted in a rational manner, in their own economic best interests, and considers that there was no logical reason for them willingly to accept sale proceeds which were lower than the purported market value of their stake. Therefore, as they were willing sellers, the proceeds and price per share accepted by them represented market value for their respective minority stakes in the appellant.

Based on the above, the shareholders were able to negotiate a larger percentage of the total transaction consideration relative to their stake after engaging in arm’s length negotiations because of their stronger negotiating position, which was largely due to them (a) having a combined majority shareholding in the appellant and acting in alliance (which gave them the power to drive liquidity events), and (b) being able to sell their majority stake separately, if and when they were more motivated to sell, compared with the other shareholders, who would not have been able to realise the price that they ultimately received for their shares, owing to their small stake of 5.77%, unless they sold as part of an overall sale of the appellant.

With reference to the “open market” within the TCGA definition, an open market is one where there are no restrictions that would prevent other potential buyers, who are able and willing, to offer a bid and complete a purchase of the shares. Each of these three sets of negotiations occurred in the open market. The market value of the shareholders’ combined stake of 50.65% must be assessed in the context of the real-world market, where all the other shareholdings in the appellant were also available for sale, given that that is what actually occurred and the actual demand at the relevant time (6 August 2014) was for 100% of the shares in the appellant.

None of the negotiating groups involved was related to any other group involved in the transaction. Each set of negotiations was undertaken separately, with the parties acting independently, with a view to maximising their own respective positions. There is nothing to suggest that any of the parties did not act in a rational manner. Each of the sellers was a willing party to the transaction and none of them were “overeager” in the sense of desperate to sell (for whatever reason) as shown, for example, if they did not follow the due process of sale, such as undertaking proper marketing, preparing information memoranda and/or allowing prospective buyers time to undertake due diligence. The most motivated to sell appears to have been Prism but Prism was not overeager. For example, Prism had marketed their stake to at least one other party and had produced an information memorandum, which is consistent with Prism following the due process of sale. Mr Maynard described the negotiations with Prism as “difficult” and he also says “it was not easy to ger Mr Carter and his colleagues at Prism to agree; they took their time”. Being difficult and engaging in lengthy negotiations is not behaviour that is consistent with being an overeager seller who is desperate to sell. He had not seen any evidence to suggest that any of the other sellers involved in the transaction were overeager or forced sellers.

He considers (a) CV was a rational buyer that would not have been willing to pay anything other than the lowest price possible to obtain 100% of the shares in the appellant, and (b) the proceeds received by each of the sellers was the best price reasonably obtainable by each seller respectively, and (c) the transaction satisfies the requirements of para 30.2 set out above. CV was a willing buyer and each seller was a willing seller. In particular, with respect to the shareholders, the price they agreed for their own shares was accepted by all the other parties, implying that it was considered to have been reasonable in the market. The shareholders satisfy the definition of willing sellers motivated to sell at the best price attainable in the open market after proper marketing. The three sets of negotiations took place between unconnected third parties, who engaged in arm’s length negotiations, each acting independently. Given that negotiations were undertaken with multiple interested parties over a period of almost four years prior to the completion of sale, it can be presumed that the parties involved in the transaction had each acted knowledgeably and prudently. No party was compelled to act in a manner that was anything other than in their economic best interests, including being forced or unduly coerced to complete the transaction. On that basis the consideration paid by the buyer and received by each of the sellers meets all the elements of the market value definition at the valuation date (6 August 2014). Since CV engaged in arm’s length negotiations with the shareholders (acting on behalf of all the sellers), and the shareholders engaged in arm’s length negotiations with the minority shareholders and the five other majority shareholders, it follows logically that the entire transaction and the proceeds received by each seller were based on arm’s length negotiations, since every negotiation that led to the transaction was at arm’s length.

Based on all of the above, he considers that the transaction and the proceeds and price per share received by the shareholders as part of the transaction represents the best indicator of the market value of their shareholding as at the valuation date (6 August 2014) and satisfies the TCGA definition of market value: (a) All the negotiating groups involved in the transaction were unrelated willing parties, acting in their own economic best interests, (b) none of the selling shareholders was under any compulsion to sell their shares at a price that they did not consider to be fair for their stake, (c) the market conditions as at the transaction date were the same as those as at the valuation date (6 August 2014); and (d) the transaction took place in the open market.

Where a valuer considers an alternative valuation approach to estimate the market value of a business, they would typically consider trading multiples of listed comparable businesses, or comparable transactions. However, in this case, given the availability of a reliable transaction involving the shareholders’ stake as at the exact valuation date based on arm’s length negotiations, there is no need to perform any further valuation exercises. As a cross-check, he considered whether it is reasonable that the shareholders’ stake had a higher market value. The three groups of selling shareholders did not sell identical instruments and had differing percentage shareholdings in the appellant. The shareholders, negotiating together, held a majority in the appellant. He considers that this size of collective shareholding gave the shareholders a significant degree of control over the appellant and therefore a stronger position when negotiating together, whereas all the other selling shareholders owned minority stakes and did not have the same degree of control. A controlling stake provides the holder with the ability to influence management and financial decisions, specifically, to initiate and complete liquidity events at their discretion such as a sale of the business. Therefore, non-controlling shareholders are in a relatively disadvantageous position and are reliant on controlling shareholders to crystallise value for them. Given the degree of control afforded to the shareholders by their controlling stake, it is reasonable that the market value of their holding would be higher on a price per share basis, as it includes the advantage of a control premium attributable to the controlling element. In addition, the position taken by the shareholders in the negotiations with the other shareholders was that they were not prepared to accept a lower price per share for their stake than what they ultimately received, and were instead willing to walk away from the sale. Their combined controlling stake and their reluctance to sell gave them an unusually powerful ability to dictate terms in this transaction. Additionally, Mr Maynard states that the shareholders would not have used the drag-along rights in the Articles to compel other shareholders to sell, as that would have meant the shareholders accepting a lower price for their shares, which they were not prepared to do. He therefore understands how the shareholders, acting as an alliance holding a combined majority stake of 50.65%, were able to negotiate a higher price per share for their controlling stake.

At the hearing Mr Weaver did not put forward any convincing rationale for his view that the negotiations between Mr Wells and Mr Maynard and the minority shareholders and the other majority shareholders can be taken as the basis of the hypothetical transaction as though Mr Wells and Mr Maynard were in the position of a buyer. He was also unable to explain with any clarity why he had referred to a number of matters in his report which he then accepted are not relevant to an assessment of the hypothetical sale transaction or the basis for assumptions and conclusions he had made:

He said, in effect, that (a) a transaction with Mr Maynard/Mr Wells on one side, trying to decrease the price, and Prism and Bond on the other side, trying to increase the price, is consistent with the hypothetical transaction; Mr Maynard and Mr Wells acted like a hypothetical buyer in those negotiations, (b) CV did not care about how the purchase price was to be allocated; they left that to the individual sellers. That converts Mr Maynard and Mr Wells into hypothetical buyers, (c) each set of negotiations involved two parties on either side of a transaction, acting for self-interest and gain and independently, where one party got more than the other party. If Prism and Bond took 5 million less, and all other things being equal, then Mr Maynard and Mr Wells would get 5 million more. That is a classic willing buyer/willing seller transaction. It is a negotiation. There were quite serious economics passing between Prism and Bond and Mr Maynard/Mr Wells. There was a commercial deal, and they were on either sides of it, and (d) it is a bit like the deal with CV. Mr Wells did that negotiation with CV, there was a price to be paid, and the flex on that price would either be for the benefit of the shareholders or, if CV negotiated a lower price, the benefit of CV. So, it is the same sort of concept, (e) whilst CV did not negotiate to buy, or make any offer to buy, 50.65%, or any other proportion less than 100%, there were “obviously separate deals for the different shareholdings. So they did ultimately sign off on what they paid for the 50.65%” and he was looking at the hypothetical transaction for 50.65% of the shares, (f) one is testing the transaction, in terms of trying to understand what the relative value drivers were between the buyers and sellers in that transaction, and (g) although he used the term allocation, it was not just that. The shareholders were negotiating against each other on either side of the relevant negotiation/allocation. There were three underlying deals which were done as a negotiation. These resulted in the prices per share that were negotiated between the relevant shareholders and resulted in a transaction with CV.

It was put to him that he is not in a position to understand the basis of the value allocation as between Mr Wells and Mr Maynard and Prism/Bond or between them and the other majority shareholders. He said that the allocation is the allocation: the deal was done between a willing buyer and a willing seller. Whilst one needs to test the transaction, ultimately, Prism and Bond agreed to the deal. When it was put to him that he had not seen documents evidencing the transactions, he said that Bond and Prism were private equity shareholders and he assumed that they asked for anything that they thought was relevant to help them decide on the deal. He could only assume that the individual shareholders asked for any material information that they needed in order to sign the deal. One of them received £14 million, so he assumed that he did appropriate due diligence. Moreover, CV wanted 100% of the shares in the appellant, so the individual had the power to say no to the deal. All of the shareholders signed the deal, that is the starting point. To him these look like negotiated deals, and the sellers did not have to sign up to it.

It was put to him that a private agreement between the shareholders does not tell one what the market value of their shares is. He said that, if the negotiations between those shareholders mirrored the hypothetical transaction, that would have occurred if they were selling the individual shareholdings, then it would be reflective of the market value. He accepted that the market value of a shareholding of say 30%, 40% or 50% if sold alone is different to the market value of that shareholding in the context of a deal for sale of the whole share capital. He said that, in this deal, CV agreed to pay £665 million for the whole of the share capital and then there were negotiations for the deals beneath that under which the relevant parties were on either side of the transaction negotiating independently. He made the uncontroversial point that one is trying to assess what a hypothetical seller would obtain in that transaction from a hypothetical buyer, with all the knowledge that they have of the deal. However, he was not able to explain why the negotiations in these deals can be taken to reflect the hypothetical sale. He said, as regards the other majority shareholders, that the hypothetical buyer knows the price which Prism and Bond have agreed to sell for which leaves £2,800 per share for the majority shareholders. In his view, they had all the information that they needed. It was put to him that the private agreement between the shareholders only shows the value which they agreed to allocate amongst themselves because of their particular circumstances, characteristics and pre-existing relationship. He said Prism and Bond accepted their price as a separately negotiated deal with Mr Maynard. If they were going out into the hypothetical market, on the basis that £665 million would be received for the total, they would agree to sell their shareholdings at what they did.

He agreed that in assessing the hypothetical transaction the fact that Prism and Bond were investors who had bought into a business at a very late stage and, in the case of Prism, had been very obstructive are particular to them, as sellers, and would be excluded in considering the hypothetical seller as would the fact that the majority shareholders had to give guarantees and warranties if they were personal to them.

He did not accept that, on Mr Wells’ evidence, Prism were an overeager seller for the purposes of paragraph 30.2(e). He said they were just keen to sell not overeager or a forced seller. He said he thought of an ‘overeager’ seller as a forced seller, rather than actually just keen to sell, despite the fact that the paragraph in the IVS states that a “willing seller” is “neither an overeager nor a forced seller”.

Nor did he accept that Mr Wells was a reluctant seller because he said he would only sell for a “spectacular” price. He said that (a) he was a willing seller who was only willing to sell at the amount that he sold at in the end to a willing buyer who would pay that price, (b) a reluctant seller is someone who is willing to accept a lower price than market price, (c) he had described them as reluctant sellers in his report in the sense of reluctant to sell at a price below the price that they were willing to accept. They might have been reluctant to sell at a specific price, but once they got to a price that they were comfortable with, they were willing sellers. Someone is not a reluctant seller provided there is a price at which they are willing to sell. They are a reluctant seller until they are a willing seller and then the deal gets done. If they sell then they are a willing seller, and (d) this is the basis on which he applied paragraph 30.2 in his report.

This evidence suggests that any party who sold an asset is a willing seller because they ultimately sold the asset. We find that Mr Weaver gave no meaningful explanation of what a “willing seller” is to be taken to be.

He accepted that the hypothetical transaction is presumed to be between unrelated parties each acting independently such that it is necessary to exclude from the assessment any value that is determined or influenced by the particular characteristics or control of a party derived from their role in the relationship. It was put to him that, in this case, there was a knowledge imbalance in the relevant relationship as the other shareholders were entirely dependent upon Mr Maynard and Mr Wells in terms of knowledge of CV’s motivations, reasoning and negotiating position. He accepted that there was such an imbalance as to how the £665 million of the total price paid by CV was reached but said that in the other negotiations (which he relied on as evidence of market value) all they were really trying to do was to allocate the £665 million. He did not accept that, in light of this, Mr Maynard and Mr Wells were not acting at arm’s length or independent of the other sellers in the negotiation as to the allocation of the £665 million.

It was put to him that the appropriate manner of marketing in the hypothetical transaction would not involve collaboration between the sellers’ sole negotiator and the buyer to structure the deal to enhance the bargaining position of one party in their negotiations with another party as was the case by the inclusion of the “forward-looking warranties”. He said (a) that was a negotiation tactic and marketing is “sort of slightly different”, (b) in the hypothetical transaction, one has to assume perfect information is given to both buyer and seller. He did not accept that the best available information, was not available to Prism and Bond. He said that what Prism and Bond thought of the £107 million is not for him and they still agreed to sell at the price they agreed to sell at. He accepted that it is important for these purposes that information which is reasonably available is not withheld from one of the parties, and provided to them promptly during the negotiations and one would expect the parties to be kept up to date during the negotiations. He said that once the negotiations for the £665 million were concluded, the negotiations were then between the shareholders. It was put to him that the agreement with CV on the price was reached, at the latest, by 26 May 2014 but the individual shareholders were not informed of that and the discussions did not start with them until 19 June 2024. He said that the key information that they needed to decide whether to accept their price was quite simply the price that CV was willing to pay, the price that Prism and Bond were willing to sell at, which gives a figure of almost £2,800 a share, and they agreed at slightly less than that. In his view, they had enough information to make their decision at the date that they did their deal, otherwise they would not have done the deal.

This evidence suggests that Mr Weaver did not consider whether these shareholders “acted knowledgeably, prudently” and were “reasonably informed about … the state of the market as of the valuation date”. Rather he simply assumed these things to be true based on the fact that these individuals had signed the deal.

He accepted that when carrying out the hypothetical transaction, one would have to exclude any value attributable to the withdrawal of the legal proceedings and he had not done that in his report and that was a flaw with it. He stated that he had not asked for any information to enable him to identify the value of the withdrawal of those proceedings.

He initially accepted that any value attributed to the management shareholders to reflect their contribution to the growth or success of the business would not be attributed to the hypothetical seller. His evidence on this was inconsistent. He then said that in the correspondence in which Mr Wells talked of being entitled to the price differential on this basis, he thought Mr Wells meant that the entire value of the appellant’s business has been created by the executives and he was saying that as a negotiation tactic. He said, in that sense, the equity value was driven by the executive shareholdings and that is not personal to them; this is business that they have created. On that basis all of the consideration of £665 million should be allocated to the management, because the entire value was attributable to them. It was put to him that if the reason why Prism or Bond agreed to accept the price differential was because, or in part, to reflect the personal work that Mr Wells and Maynard had put in to build up the business, that would not reflect the market value of their shares. He said the price in the hypothetical transaction is based on the future rather than the history and he did not think any buyer or seller really cares what the management have done in the past. They are just buying the future cashflows and that has nothing to do with the value that was created in the past. He said:

p.span: “you’ve got to put yourself into the position of a willing seller selling these shareholdings, Prism and Bond, and you’re looking at all the information that is in the market, and this is a negotiating tactic that Mr Maynard and Mr Wells have put forth, and they’ve agreed to the price that they’ve agreed. This was one of the things they talked of in the negotiation.”

blockContainer.p: In our view, it is plain that for the purposes of the test in ss 272 and 273 and the IVS Guidelines the value which a party places on their contribution to building a business is a matter personal to them which would not be taken account of in assessing a hypothetical sale. Mr Weaver’s point that, in a sense, all the value of the business is attributable to the efforts of the executives who work in it is nothing to the point. The point is that in fact Mr Wells and Mr Maynard sought to justify the price differential on the basis that they deserved the price differential as a reward for their role in the business.

He accepted that, when determining the market value of shares, the rights attaching to those shares are an important consideration and shares which have the same rights would ordinarily be expected to have the same value to the hypothetical buyer who wishes to buy the entire share capital. He was asked what relevance there was to his report that he had highlighted that Bond had preference shares given that ordinarily such shares may be worth more rather than less than the ordinary shares. He said again that there were three separate negotiations for different assets (the preference shares, in the case of Bond, ordinary and A ordinary shares, in the case of Prism, and ordinary shares as regards the other shareholders). So there were three different deals, which have to be looked at separately and the basis for them understood. He assumed CV knew that they were acquiring preference shares from Bond and that was the deal done for those shares. He said the fact that Prism and Bond received the same price for their shares simply showed that the value of their respective shareholdings was the same. He said that one has to consider all of the rights that a preference shareholder owns and those rights would have been considered in the deal; this is a private equity investor who must have known the nature of the asset that they owned.
Mr Weaver was not able to explain how the difference in the share rights was relevant or how it impacted the price obtained by the different shareholders in this case.

He accepted that it is not appropriate to take account in the required market value exercise of (a) the pre-emption rights relating to the other majority shareholders as, from the actual buyer’s perspective, those rights did nothing to diminish the value of the shares held by those individuals in its hands following the acquisition, (b) the fact that Prism may have only received a smaller amount if it sold its shareholding individually, (c) whether the hypothetical parties would be pleased or disappointed with the result by reference to what the property might be worth at a different time or in different circumstance, (d) and the fact that Prism had come to the end of its seven-year fund period, with a hard stop in two years, and therefore were keen to sell their fund and exit their investment as soon as possible, as the hypothetical seller would not necessarily have the same characteristics. Those are special circumstances that relate to this particular seller which might explain why they were willing to accept less than the market value for these shares, and (e) the return of investment made by a particular buyer, either in isolation or compared to the multiples that would have been achieved by other investments. He added that that is not relevant to the hypothetical transaction but it is a good and helpful benchmark for testing the actual deals that were done in this particular case. It was put to him that, in determining whether or not Prism was an overeager seller, he took into account the very thing that he accepts is irrelevant. He said that he was trying to test whether they were overeager in the actual transaction that he was using as a benchmark for the hypothetical transaction.
Mr Weaver could not explain why he had taken into account the return on investment only in the case of Prism, but not as regards the other shareholders.

It was put to him that there is no evidence that the minority shareholders had to persuade the shareholders to sell their controlling stake as part of the transaction. He agreed but said he was just explaining in his report that they did not have the power to force a deal. He could not explain why he made this assumption but eventually accepted that “persuade might not be the right word”. He added that the shareholders had to agree to sell their stake for the business to be sold at 100%. It was put to him that he was relying on the fact that Mr Wells was a reluctant seller. He said that Mr Wells and Mr Maynard had to agree to sell their stake for the minority shareholders to obtain the benefit of a sale and he was reluctant until he was willing. He signed the deal.

It was put to him that in his report he had erred as he had not considered the highest price that the hypothetical buyer would pay. He said that the conclusion is that that deal was done at the lowest price that the sellers would agree and at a price that the shareholders were willing to accept. He said that there was a seller and a representative acting on the other side of the transaction negotiating a deal, and they agreed a price; he was talking about the deal that was done between them as there were two actual parties to the transaction, and that is the end of the market value analysis. He does not see how a hypothetical transaction would not actually play out exactly as this transaction played out; because these actual sellers agreed to that price, therefore, that is the market value.

It was put to him (a) he does not mention or take into account the fact that Mr Maynard justified the difference in price per share to the other majority shareholders by emphasising that he and Mr Wells were giving warranties and undertakings which they did not have to give, and (b) those are special and particular circumstances that relate only to Mr Wells and Mr Maynard and Mrs Maynard in their personal capacity. He said they were really giving them on behalf of the company and “there’s nothing personal to them”. He then accepted that these and the other circumstances Mr Maynard stated to the other shareholders “are all special circumstances which are unrelated to the shares or the rights attaching to the shares” and any value, therefore, attributable to those special circumstances would have to be excluded from the market value transaction and this would explain why these particular shareholders agreed to accept less. He said that he did not think there was much value in them. He noted that there is £1.5 million attributed to warranty and indemnity insurance which could probably be taken as the value of those warranties because it was the premium that was paid to indemnify them away. As regards the escrow he said the loss of investment opportunity on £14 million, assuming the funds are returned, is interest on £14 million.

p.span: Parties’ written submissions on the admissibility of Mr Weaver’s evidence

blockContainer.p: HMRC referred to the decision in De Sena and anor v Notaro and ors [2021] 1 BCLC 366 (“De Sena”), where Judge Paul Matthews (sitting as a Judge of the High Court) summarised the basic principles relevant to expert evidence at [150] as follows:

p.span: “Most evidence given at trial is evidence of
fact
. As a general proposition, evidence of
opinion
is not admissible. But
expert

opinion evidence is an exception to this general rule, now governed by s 3(1) of the Civil Evidence Act 1972. Expert evidence is a common and usually a helpful feature of modern litigation. As its name suggests, and as provided for by s 3(1), it is different from evidence of
fact
in that it involves the witness, who must possess sufficient expertise in the relevant subject-matter, giving his or her
opinion
as to one or more issues arising in the proceedings.”

blockContainer.p: HMRC noted that Judge Matthews also said that: “The court’s direction cannot make inadmissible evidence admissible” (see [154(2)]).

HMRC submitted, as the appellant did not appear to dispute, that whilst there is no specific rule in the Rules that mirrors CPR 35.1, the tribunal should take account of the case law based on the rule in CPR 35.1 (see Singleton Birch Ltd and anor v HMRC [2022] SFTD 433 at [9]). They referred to the decision in Kennedy v Cordia (Services) LLP [2016] 1 WLR 611 (“Kennedy”), where Lords Reed and Hodge set out the following principles:
At [39] to [41], they noted that not only can skilled witnesses give evidence of their opinions, they can also give skilled evidence of fact:

p.span: “based on his or her knowledge and experience of the subject matter, drawing on the work of others, such as the findings of a published research or the pooled knowledge of a team of people with whom he or she works”.

blockContainer.p: They said that the special rules that govern admissibility of expert opinion evidence also cover such skilled evidence of fact, being, as set out at [44]:

p.span: whether the proposed skilled evidence will assist the court in its task;
whether the witness has the necessary knowledge and experience;
whether the witness is impartial in his or her presentation and assessment of the evidence; and
whether there is a reliable body of knowledge or experience to underpin the expert’s evidence.”

blockContainer.p: At [45] they said:
“It is for the court to decide whether expert evidence is needed, when the admissibility of that evidence is challenged”.
“If on the proven facts a judge or jury can form their own conclusions without help, then the opinion of an expert is unnecessary” (quoting R v Turner (Terence) [1975] QB 834 per Lawton LJ).

“The subject matter under discussion must be necessary such that a judge or jury without instruction or advice in the particular area of knowledge or experience would be unable to reach a sound conclusion without the help of a witness who had such specialised knowledge or experience” (quoting Wilson v HM Advocate 2009 JC 336 per Lord Wheatley).

They continued, at [46], that strict necessity cannot be the test for the admissibility of skilled evidence of fact as otherwise the court could be “deprived of the benefit of a skilled witness who collates and presents to the court in an efficient manner the knowledge of others in his or her field of expertise”. There may be circumstances in which a court could determine a fact in issue without an expert collation of relevant facts if the parties called many factual witnesses at great expense such that a strict necessity test would not be met. They referred to a decision of the United States Supreme Court (Daubert v Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals Inc (1993) 509 US 579) on a rule of evidence which, in their view, is consistent with the approach of Scots law in relation to skilled evidence of fact:

mainBody.p: “If scientific, technical or other specialized knowledge will assist the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue, a witness qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education, may testify thereto in the form of an opinion or otherwise.”

blockContainer.p: They concluded, at [47], that the advantage of the formula in this rule is that:

mainBody.p: “it avoids an over-rigid interpretation of necessity where a skilled witness is put forward to present relevant factual evidence in an efficient manner rather than give an opinion explaining the factual evidence of others. If skilled evidence of fact would be likely to assist the efficient determination of the case, the judge should admit it.”

blockContainer.p: They continued, at [48] and [49], that an expert must explain the basis of his or her evidence “when it is not personal observation or sensation”; mere assertion “is worthless”. In addition, expert witness evidence “cannot usurp the functions of the jury or the judge sitting as a jury”. Thus, while on occasion, in order to avoid illusive language, the skilled witness may have to express his or her views in a way that addresses the ultimate issue for the court, expert assistance does not extend to supplanting the court as the decision-maker. The fact-finding judge cannot delegate the decision-making role to the expert.

Finally, at [51], they noted that the court may exclude expert evidence which “on its face does not comply with the recognised duties of a skilled witness to be independent and impartial”. In their view that requirement was “one of admissibility rather than merely of the weight of the evidence…”

HMRC also referred to [151] of De Sena where, it was stated that, as set out in Kennedy at [49] “… the expert cannot usurp the functions of the court in finding the facts or interpreting the law” and that:

mainBody.p: “Moreover, and importantly, expert evidence must be restricted to that which is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings: CPR 35.1. Mere desirability or helpfulness is not enough: see British Airways plc v Spencer [2015] EWHC 2477 (Ch), [2015] All ER (D) 101 (Aug), at [68].” (Emphasis added.)

blockContainer.p: The appellant noted that, at [150] of De Sena, Judge Matthews set out that an expert witness is to “assume the facts for the purposes of giving such opinion evidence: see JP Morgan Chase Bank v Springwell Navigation Corp [2006] EWHC 2755 (Comm), [2007] 1 All ER (Comm) 549 at [21]”. In [21] of the JP Morgan case cited in this passage, Aikens J (as he then was) said this:

mainBody.p: “Although in former years it was said that experts should not give opinions on “the very issue which the court has to decide”, that restriction is no longer in force, at least in civil actions: see Barings Plc (In Liquidation) v Coopers & Lybrand [2001] Lloyds LR (Banking) 85 at para 54 per Evans-Lombe J and the cases there cited. However, it is not for experts to attempt to make findings of fact. Instead, they should express their opinion on the area in which they have their expertise on the basis of assumed facts which should be clearly identified and stated in their expert report.” (Emphasis added.)

blockContainer.p: More recently in Griffiths v TUI (UK) Ltd [2023] 3 WLR 1204 at [36], Lord Hodge has reinforced the fact that the expert must not usurp the functions of the judge:

mainBody.p: “It is trite law that the role of an expert is to assist the court in relation to matters of scientific, technical or other specialised knowledge which are outside the judge’s expertise by giving evidence of fact or opinion; but the expert must not usurp the functions of the judge as the ultimate decision-maker on matters that are central to the outcome of the case.” (Emphasis added.)

blockContainer.p: Both parties referred to the decision of the tribunal in Hastings Insurance Services Ltd v HMRC [2018] UKFTT 27 (TC) (“Hastings”). In that case, the question was whether the taxpayer’s supplies of insurance services to its client were made in the UK and thus exempt supplies for VAT purposes, or in Gibraltar (see [5]). HMRC sought to produce an expert report from a UK solicitor, which opined on where the services were supplied (see [36]). The tribunal concluded, at [57], that the majority of the report was inadmissible as it was either “legal opinion” or it “sought to address the very issues for the tribunal”. At [60], the tribunal explained that the expert:

p.span: “… simply gave his own views on the factual evidence and drew his own legal conclusions from that evidence and his own construction of the effect of the contractual arrangements between the parties. …given the way the questions he was asked to address were phrased (being the very VAT questions the tribunal has to answer) and the manner in which he expressed his conclusions, in many sections he appeared to address the very legal question before the tribunal on the basis of his own view of the facts and law.”

blockContainer.p: The appellant noted that the expert’s evidence was not fully excluded but admitted in part (see [62]).

In Hastings at [45] the tribunal referred to the fact that the “no usurpation” principle referred to in Kennedy was also recognised in this tribunal in Deloitte LLP v HMRC [2016] UKFTT 479 (TC) (“Deloitte”) where:

p.span: “the tribunal drew a distinction between opinions “whose foundation is built on matters which are outside the tribunal’s expertise” and opinions “whose foundation itself rests on legal matters which are properly for the tribunal to reach a conclusion on with the benefit of the relevant facts and legal submission …”

blockContainer.p: The appellant also referred to Singleton Birch Ltd and anor v HMRC [2022] SFTD 433 (“Singleton”), a case in which the taxpayer sought to have expert evidence excluded, partly on the basis that the report usurped the role of the tribunal:
At [18], the tribunal identified the following principles set out in Deloitte, which it then accepted and adopted:

p.span: Relevant evidence should be admitted unless there are compelling reasons not to. The prejudice to each party of respectively admitting/not admitting the evidence should be weighed. (
Mobile Export365
and
Atlantic Electronic
An expert's evidence of opinion is admissible because it is the product of a special expertise which the tribunal does not possess, or even if it does, which is not its function to apply ([
Rogers v Hoyle

Expert reports are not rendered inadmissible because they refer to legislation, matters of law or indeed the very issue before the court or tribunal. Tribunal panels (who are not lay finders of fact) can be credited with the ability to distinguish between inadmissible / admissible matters in a report and to know that they have to reach their own view on the legal question before them. (
JP Morgan Chase Bank
, and
Kennedy

Even if reports contain inadmissible expert evidence of fact they can be admitted and should be admitted without requiring excision particularly if the admissible/ inadmissible evidence of fact is intertwined
(Hoyle

blockContainer.p: At [19], the tribunal said: “…where the question is one of law, expert evidence will be excluded because that is within the expertise of the court and expert evidence does not assist.” At [20], the tribunal cited the following passages from esure Insurance Ltd v Direct Line Insurance plc [2008] EWCA Civ 842 (“esure”):

p.span: “[75] It is, of course, permissible for an expert to opine on the ultimate question if it is one of fact, not law, as I said in my judgment (with the concurrence of the other members of the Court) in
Rockwater v Coflexip
, [2004] EWCA Civ 381, [2004] RPC 46. I repeat part of it here:
[13] But it also is permissible for an expert witness to opine on an 'ultimate question' which is not one of law. I so held in
Routestone Ltd v Minories Finance Ltd
[1997] B.C.C. 180 and see s.3 of the Civil Evidence Act 1972.

[14] But just because the opinion is admissible, it by no means follows that the court must follow it. On its own (unless uncontested) it would be 'a mere bit of empty rhetoric' Wigmore, Evidence (Chadbourn rev) para.1920. What really matters in most cases is the reasons given for the opinion. As a practical matter a well-constructed expert's report containing opinion evidence sets out the opinion and the reasons for it. If the reasons stand up the opinion does, if not, not.”
[76] Assertions of the sort I have set out seem to me to fall within that vivid phrase, “empty rhetoric” and are of no value.”

blockContainer.p: At [92] the tribunal in Singleton reiterated the foregoing, saying that: “Both esure and Deloitte confirm that an expert may give his opinion on the ultimate issues of facts. ...” (emphasis in original).
At [93], the tribunal cited the passage from Hastings at [45] in which the tribunal referred to Deloitte (as set out above).

The appellant submitted that the caselaw shows that (1) when considering whether an expert report is “usurping” the function of the tribunal, it is clear that experts can opine on matters of fact and on the “ultimate question” provided that it is one of fact, not one of law, (2) an example of such a case is expert accountancy evidence as to what comprises Generally Accepted Accounting Practice (“GAAP”), for example, as regards the profits of a trade which statute states are to be calculated in accordance with GAAP, (3) accountants are very frequently called to give expert evidence to assist with determining what the appropriate GAAP is and how the profits in question should be calculated in accordance with it, (4) accountants giving such evidence are, thus, opining on the “ultimate question” every time they give expert evidence to the tribunal, and (5) such evidence is readily admissible and admitted all the time. There is a clear parallel with valuation evidence. Although this term appears in the statutory wording, and is the very thing that the tribunal has to assess, it is established that the issue is one of fact, not law, “to be determined with the assistance of expert evidence”: Ball UK Holdings Ltd v HMRC [2018] UKUT 407 (TCC) at [40].

The appellant referred to Phones 4U Ltd v EE Ltd & Ors [2021] EWHC 2879 (Ch) (“Phones 4U”), a competition case concerning alleged economic collusion, in which the claimant sought permission to call expert evidence from an economist. It was held that there are two stages of determining whether expert evidence is reasonably required (see [11]).
