The first stage is to consider “whether there is a recognised body of expertise governed by recognised standards and rules of conduct relevant to the question which the Court has to decide” (see [11] and [12]). As regards the second stage, at [15] the Court cited with approval the following passages from the judgment in British Airways plc v Spencer [2015] EWHC 2477 (Ch) (“British Airways”) at [63] and [68]:

p.span: … A judgment needs to be made in every case and, in making that judgment, it is relevant to consider whether, on the one hand, the evidence is necessary (in the sense that a decision cannot be made without it) or whether it is of very marginal relevance with the court being well able to decide the issue without it, in which case a balance has to be struck and the proportionality of its admission assessed. In striking that balance, the court should, in my judgment, be prepared to take into account disparate factors including the value of the claim, the effect of a judgment either way on the parties, who is to pay for the commissioning of the evidence on each side and the delay, if any, which the production of such evidence would entail (particularly delay which might result in the vacating of a trial date).

… it is necessary to look at the pleaded issues and, unless and until a particular issue is excluded from consideration under CPR 3.1(2)(k), the court must ask itself the following important questions:
The first question is whether, looking at each issue,
it is necessary for there to be
expert evidence before that issue can be resolved. If it is necessary, rather than merely
helpful, it seems to me that it must be admitted
If the evidence is not necessary, the second question is whether it would be of assistance to the court in resolving that issue.
If it would be of assistance, but not necessary, then the court would be able to determine the issue without it (just as in
Mitchell
the court would have been able to resolve even the central issue without the expert evidence).

Since, under the scenario in (b) above, the court will be able to resolve the issue without the evidence, the third question is whether, in the context of the proceedings as a whole, expert evidence on that issue is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings. In that case, the sort of questions I have identified in paragraph 63 above will fall to be taken into account. In addition, in the present case, there is the complication that a particular piece of expert evidence may go to more than one pleaded issue, or evidence necessary for one issue may need only slight expansion to cover another issue where it would be of assistance but not necessary.” (Emphasis added.)

blockContainer.p: The appellant noted that it was stated in the British Airways case at [8] that “what is reasonably required is informed by the overriding objective and that the court should not be over-zealous in excluding evidence in order to save time and cost”.

HMRC submitted that Mr Weaver’s evidence is inadmissible because it is not reasonably required to resolve the market value issue. In this case, a sale of the shares did in fact occur on the valuation date. The tribunal’s task is to decide between two positions:

(a) Whether, as is HMRC’s position, the market value of the shares held by the shareholders is equal to the total consideration paid by CV, divided by the total number of shares in the appellant, or (b) whether, as is the appellant’s position, the price actually received by each shareholder represents the market value of their shares.

The tribunal’s decision on this issue depends on its interpretation and application of ss 272 and 273 TCGA, construed purposively, to the facts of this case, viewed realistically. To reach its decision the tribunal will be required to resolve various questions of law; expert evidence is not reasonably required for the tribunal to resolve any of them. The questions are:

When determining market value in circumstances where a purchaser agrees to buy all the shares in the company for a global figure, can one shareholding be worth more than another shareholding of the same class?

In such circumstances, is it appropriate to substitute the private agreement among sellers for the open market test, which is designed to identify the highest price reasonably obtainable by the hypothetical seller/the highest price a reasonably prudent purchaser would pay? In determining market value, is it relevant to take into account the subjective views or approaches of particular shareholders in allocating the division of the sale proceeds among themselves?

For the purpose of identifying the market value of the shares held by the shareholders in the hypothetical transaction between a hypothetical seller and buyer (see Gray), and in circumstances where CV negotiated and agreed to buy all the shares in the appellant, is it appropriate to draw an analogy with the situation in which “a purchaser comes along and wants to buy a company which is held across diverse ownership, and has to go along to each parcel of shares and agree with the holder a price for which they’re willing to dispose of their shares” (as the appellant submitted).

For the purpose of determining market value, what factors are extrinsic to the shares and therefore irrelevant to the determination of market value? In particular, is it permissible to take into account reasons for the special price received by the shareholders which related to their particular circumstances? (See Grays Timber at 43 D).

In some, perhaps even many, cases involving the determination of market value of an asset, expert valuation evidence will be reasonably required to resolve the proceedings. But this case is unusual. The assets in question were sold on the valuation date, and the tribunal’s task is to decide which of two analyses of the transaction that took place on that date yields the correct market value for the shares in question. That is not a question for expert evidence. On the facts of this case, Mr Weaver’s report does not assist the tribunal.

The fact that Mr Weaver’s report includes a summary of para 30 of IVS 104 does not alter that position. The tribunal does not reasonably require an understanding of IVS 104 to resolve the market value issue in this case, since that standard merely distils the key principles from ss 272 and 273 TCGA and the case law on market value. In particular:

The statement in para 30.2(a) of IVS 104 that market value is “the best price reasonably obtainable by the seller and the most advantageous price reasonably obtainable by the buyer” reflects the decision in Gray where, at 372b, Hoffmann LJ stated that “the concept of the open market involves assuming that the whole world was free to bid, and then forming a view about what in those circumstances would in real life have been the best price reasonably obtainable”.
The reference in para 30.2(b) of IVS 104 to the market value being “an estimated amount” reflects that the market value under s 272 TCGA is an estimate (see s 272(2)).

The statement in para 30.2(c) of IVS 104 that the valuation must be carried out as at the valuation date is self-evident, but in any event it was stated in Gray at [372] that on “the assumption that [the hypothetical vendor and purchaser] must have behaved as one would reasonably expect of prudent parties who had in fact agreed a sale on the relevant date”.

The definition of “willing buyer” in para 30.2(d) of IVS 104 as neither over-eager nor determined to buy at any price reflects the statement in Walton (ex’or of Walton dec’d) v IRC [1996] STC 68, at 85 that “whilst both the seller and the buyer are assumed to be willing, neither is taken to be over-eager”.

The reference in para 30.2(d) of IVS 104 to the need to take into account “the realities of the current market” reflects the statement in Lynall at 153 that the hypothetical sale “should build upon a foundation of reality, so far as this is possible”.

The definition of “willing seller” in para 30.2(e) of IVS 104 reflects authorities such as Gray where, at 372a-b, Hoffmann LJ said that: “the hypothetical vendor is an anonymous but reasonable vendor, who goes about the sale as a prudent man of business, negotiating seriously without giving the impression of being either over-anxious or unduly reluctant”.

The assumption in para 30.2(f) of IVS 104 that the hypothetical transaction is one at “arm’s length” reflects the wording of s 273(3), which requires it to be assumed that the prospective purchaser had available “all the information which a prudent prospective purchaser of the asset might reasonably require if he were proposing to purchase it from a willing vendor by private treaty and at arm's length” (emphasis added).

The stipulation in para 30.2(g) of IVS 104 that the hypothetical transaction must be assumed to have taken place “after proper marketing” reflects the comment of Lord Reid in Duke of Buccleuch v IRC [1967] AC 506 at 525B that: “The commissioners must estimate what the property would probably have fetched on that particular day if it had then been exposed for sale, no doubt after such advance publicity as would have been reasonable” (emphasis added).

The assumption in para 30.2(h) of IVS 104 that the parties acted “knowledgeably, prudently” reflects Findlay’s Trustees v CIR (1938) ATC 437 where, at 440, Lord Fleming said that: “it must be assumed…that the purchaser is a person of reasonable prudence, who has informed himself with regard to all the relevant facts…”.

The requirement in para 30.2(i) of IVS 104 to assume that each party acted “without compulsion” reflects the principle in the case-law (such as in Walton, cited above) that the hypothetical seller and buyer are assumed to be willing parties.

Mr Weaver’s conclusions in section 5 of the report are based on his purported application of IVS 104, which is itself based on the case-law principles. The report’s use of IVS 104 does not provide the tribunal with any assistance that it reasonably requires.

The position is the same in relation the Guidelines to which Mr Weaver refers. There is no suggestion in the report that the criteria for assessment of fair value in those Guidelines are materially different from those required to assess market value under IVS 104. In any event, there is no reference to the Guidelines in the concluding section 5 of the report.

The fact that Mr Weaver’s evidence is not reasonably required to resolve proceedings is supported by the treatment of that evidence in the appellant’s skeleton argument. Having summarised the case-law principles, the skeleton sets out the reasons why, “in accordance with the principles summarised above”, the prices agreed by the various shareholders represents market value. The submissions are made without reference to Mr Weaver’s report. As an afterthought, the appellant states that: “These submissions are supported by the expert evidence adduced by the Appellant”. That highlights the fact that the appellant’s submissions are put in reliance on legal principles, not Mr Weaver’s report, which adds nothing to those submissions.

This case is similar to Grays Timber, which was resolved without expert evidence (see the Special Commissioner’s decision, [2009] STC 889, at [4]). There, the question for the court was whether the value of Mr Gibson’s shares was £1.4m or the rateable part of the sale proceeds, which was just under £0.4m (see [1]). That case was resolved without expert evidence. There, as here, expert evidence was not reasonably required to resolve the question of whether the market value was (a) the price actually received by the shareholder or (b) his pro rata portion of the total consideration for the company’s shares.
Conversely, this case is materially different to other cases in which valuation evidence has been relied upon to assist the tribunal’s determination of market value:

In Netley there was no disposal of the shares to a third party for value; the case concerned the value of shares that the taxpayer had gifted to charity (see [1], [3] and [4]). In those different circumstances, expert evidence was adduced by both parties to assist the tribunal in valuing the shares. The two experts, who gave substantially different valuations (see [228]), based them on detailed consideration of a range of factors (see [232] and [235]) including dealings in the shares in the period up to the valuation date, a comparable transaction, and the experts’ analysis of the company’s cashflow and price/earnings ratios. That was an exercise in which the tribunal would potentially have been assisted by expert evidence (although Judge Cannan ultimately attached greater significance to the underlying evidence than the experts’ opinions (see [231]).

In Close v HMRC [2022] UKFTT 193 (TC), similarly, the appellants gifted shares to charity (see [1]). HMRC relied on expert evidence (see [8]). The expert “identified three recognised approaches to the valuation of the business, which he described as the cost approach, the income approach and the market approach” (see [77]). Here, by contrast, Mr Weaver acknowledges that given that an actual sale of the shares occurred in this case, “there is no need to perform any further valuation exercises such as the Income Approach or the Market Approach based on comparable businesses or comparable transactions” to estimate market value”.

In Hawkings-Byass the taxpayers disposed of their shares in March 1988 (see [1]); the question was what the value of those shares had been six years earlier, in March 1982, when they were deemed to have disposed of and reacquired their holdings at their then market value for the purpose of calculating CGT indexation allowance (see [3]). In the absence of an actual disposal of the shares on the relevant valuation date, it can readily be seen why expert valuation evidence was reasonably required for the Special Commissioners to resolve proceedings in that case.
On their second contention, HMRC said the following:
The question Mr Weaver was instructed to answer is precisely the question for the tribunal to determine. Mr Weaver explains that he was asked:

p.span: Were the Relevant Shareholders’ shares disposed of for an amount which exceeded the market value of those shares at the time of their disposal b) If so, what is the amount of the excess?”

blockContainer.p: The report is replete with Mr Weaver’s own findings of fact, which go far beyond the making of assumptions and involve him descending into the arena. The findings are based on a view of the evidence that is both incomplete and untested in cross-examination. Examples of purported findings of fact include the following:
“It is clear from the evidence … that the Transaction was the product of three separate negotiations”.

“I consider that it is reasonable to consider these three sets of negotiations as separate. This is further supported by the different SPAs and the signed deeds between the three negotiating groups of sellers”.

“As far as commercial negotiations were concerned, both Private Equity Shareholders willingly agreed to accept the prices offered for the instruments held by them”, a finding for which Mr Weaver relies on Mr Maynard’s witness statement.
“The outcome of the negotiation between the Relevant Shareholders and the Private Equity Shareholders seems reasonable to me based on Mr J Maynard’s report that …”.

“… I consider that Prism was a willing seller who accepted the proceeds and price per share that they ultimately received for their stake and were satisfied that the price paid was the highest that they could have reasonably achieved for their shares considering their rights”.

“There is no evidence to suggest that the Five Other Individual Shareholders were related to each other or to any of the other parties involved in the Transaction, or that they were under any compulsion to sell their shares at that time or as part of the Transaction. Therefore, I presume that they acted in a rational manner i.e. in their own economic best interests, and I consider that there was no logical reason for them to willingly accept sale proceeds which were lower than the purported market value of their stake, as per HMRC’s argument”.
“I consider that the Relevant Shareholders were able to negotiate a larger percentage of the total Transaction consideration relative to their stake after engaging in arm’s length negotiations …”.

In fact, the whole of section 4 of the report, like much of section 3.2, simply sets out Mr Weaver’s own findings of fact. The only paragraphs of the report in which Mr Weaver relies on his experience (and, in particular, experience that the tribunal itself may not have) to make factual findings are 4.2.4, 4.2.5 and 4.3.5.

Mr Weaver sets out a “List of Information Relied Upon” on in his report which shows that he has relied on a small fraction of the documentation in making his factual findings. He has taken the appellant’s evidence at face value, without having heard it tested in cross-examination. By purporting to make findings, instead of mere assumptions of the kind on which an expert is expected to base his or her conclusions, Mr Weaver has descended into the arena and usurped the role of the tribunal.

As stated above, IVS 104 merely distils the relevant legal principles that the tribunal is bound to apply. The instructions given to Mr Weaver include a lengthy “Summary of legal principles”. These matters indicate the quasi-judicial nature of the exercise in which Mr Weaver has engaged.

Mr Weaver’s report then seeks to apply the legal principles encapsulated in IVS 104 to the detailed primary facts he has found and the inferences he has drawn from them. That is precisely the task the tribunal is required to perform.

Like the expert in Hastings, Mr Weaver “simply [gives] his own views on the factual evidence and [draws] his own legal conclusions from that evidence and his own construction of the effect of the contractual arrangements between the parties”, and his report “address[es] the very legal question before the tribunal on the basis of his own view of the facts and law”.
Mr Weaver’s own description of his report at 3.2.4 highlights the ways in which the report usurps the tribunal’s role:

mainBody.p: “In the next sections of this report, I assess the facts and circumstances surrounding the Transaction against paragraphs 30.2 (a) to (i) of IVS 104, the TCGA definition of market value (as set out in section 2) and the IPEV Guidelines relating to the Price of a Recent Investment valuation technique, to assess whether there is any reason why the actual proceeds received by the Relevant Shareholders as part of the Transaction cannot be relied on as representing market value as at the valuation date, or whether any adjustments would need to be made.”

blockContainer.p: Viewed in light of the fact that the relevant paragraph of IVS 104 reflects the case law on market value under s 272 TCGA, Mr Weaver’s description of his task here is merely a description of the tribunal’s own task of (a) “assessing the facts and circumstances surrounding the Transaction” against the relevant law, and (c) to assess whether or not the actual proceeds received by the shareholders represent market value.

HMRC added that they have long made clear their position that expert evidence is not required to resolve this case. They noted that, as set out above, on 5 May 2022, HMRC indicated to the tribunal that it did not propose to rely upon expert evidence. Although on 22 November 2023, HMRC then indicated that they did intend to rely on expert evidence, on 26 January 2024, well before the 23 February 2024 deadline for service of a report, HMRC confirmed that they would not be relying on expert evidence. HMRC said this remains their position:

p.span: “Having reviewed the position, we consider that the question whether the shares were sold for ‘market value’ within the meaning of [the relevant provisions] is not properly a matter for expert opinion on the facts of this case; it is simply a matter of applying established case law to the facts as found. This is an exercise for the Tribunal to undertake and any report purporting to do that exercise is usurping the
function of the Tribunal.”

blockContainer.p: The appellant made the following submissions on HMRC’s first ground that the expert evidence is not admissible:

It is not open to HMRC to raise the “reasonably required” criterion at this late stage. It ought to have been raised, considered and determined at the stage when permission for expert evidence was sought. In fact, permission has already been granted by the tribunal with the consent of HMRC. Moreover, this is a case where HMRC (a) have had notice for two and a half years that the appellant would rely on expert evidence, (b) have had the evidence itself for over a year, and (c) have only applied to exclude the evidence mid-way through a two-week trial. It is far too late for HMRC to submit, over a year after the evidence has been commissioned, paid for, and given to HMRC, and at a trial which was listed for two weeks in part to accommodate the expert evidence, that such evidence is not “reasonably required”. In substance, HMRC are seeking retrospectively to vary the tribunal’s directions, for which the parties jointly applied almost three years ago, to prohibit expert evidence after it has been produced and served. For that reason alone, this ground of HMRC’s application should be dismissed.

In any event, the expert evidence is “reasonably required” to determine the market value issue, having regard both to the relevant question posed by the statute and the various factors set out in British Airways and cited with approval in Phones 4U. Matters of valuation concern matters of fact and expert opinion. That is the position whether judged by reference to: (a) common sense, (b) authority, or (c) HMRC’s own internal manuals.

Section 272 TCGA seeks a “price” – a number, as a matter of fact; it is not a matter of law, as is evident from the fact that one will not find the answer to the question posed by s 272 (what is the price?) in a statute or in case law or in a legal textbook. Further, it is established as a matter of authority that matters of valuation involve matters of fact and of expert opinion. See:
IRC v Stenhouse’s Trustees [1992] STC 103 (“Stenhouse”) at p.109h-j:

mainBody.p: “It is true, as the trustees argued, that the objective is to ascertain the hypothetical value of the property in a hypothetical sale between hypothetical vendor and purchaser. It is also true that it is necessary to define, as a matter of law, the assumptions which the valuer must make. For example, in the case of Re Lynall itself, it was necessary to define the type of information which, the purchaser is to be assumed to have. Beyond that, however, valuation seems to me to be a matter of fact and expert opinion. …”

blockContainer.p: Administrators of the Estate of Caton (deceased) v Couch [1995] STC (SCD) 34 at 51d-e:

mainBody.p: “In reaching a decision about the value of the shares I have in mind the dicta of Lord Fleming in Salvesen’s Trustees when he said ((1930) 9 ATC 43 at 45):

p.span: ‘The estimation of the value of shares by a highly artificial standard which is never applied in the ordinary share market must be a matter of opinion and does not admit of precise scientific or mathematical calculation.’”

blockContainer.p: Netley at [230]:

p.span: “I do not consider that is the right approach to expert evidence on valuation. The experts are not saying what they would pay for the shares if they were a prospective purchaser. Their evidence is directed to what, in their reasoned opinion, the hypothetical prudent purchaser would pay based on the information available. The market value is a single price, ascertained through a process of valuation. Mr Firth’s approach seeks to place a burden on HMRC to satisfy the tribunal that the appellant’s expert has been unreasonable. In my view there is no justification for such an approach. The ultimate question based on all the evidence, including that of both experts, is what the hypothetical prudent purchaser would pay in the open market.”

blockContainer.p: Moreover, HMRC say that matters of valuation are matters of opinion in their own Shares and Assets Valuation Manual at SVM113030:

p.span: “The statutory open market basis of valuation is set out at SVM113010…Given the relative brevity of the statutory provisions, it is hardly surprising that a body of case law has built up over the years to interpret and apply the legislation. The fiscal valuer needs to have a thorough knowledge and good understanding of the legal framework that has been established by both statute and case law.

It is important to put the decisions of the tax tribunals and courts in valuation disputes into proper context. The role of a judge is to apply the law to the facts of a particular case. Having decided how the law operates, the judge then has to settle the valuation dispute by reference to the evidence, including any expert evidence, presented about the asset to be valued. Of course, that evidence will rest on the particular facts of each case as they stood at the valuation date, the valuation conditions and perceptions in place at that time, and the respective views expressed by any expert witnesses. The judge may make law as to the appropriate interpretation of the statutory valuation hypothesis but judicial decisions on particular valuation techniques such as discounts from company value for minority holdings; for unmarketability; or for the possibility of a future sale are not matters of binding law. Just as it is inappropriate to reduce share valuation to overly simplistic guidelines, it is misleading to think that the decided cases necessarily provide firm pointers for the selection of valuation techniques or data. Of course, they may indeed be interesting and, even, relevant. Please consider these points when using this chapter.”

blockContainer.p: Accordingly, while the legislation sets out the applicable definition of “market value” and prescribes certain assumptions to be made in performing the valuation (along with the assumptions required by the case law), what s 272 TCGA ultimately seeks is a “price”. That is a question of fact and expert opinion. The statutory machinery and the guidance from the case law are only parameters for the estimation of that question of fact, as the Court of Session observed in Stenhouse.
In light of the principles set out above:
There can be no suggestion that valuation is not a recognised or established field of expertise.

As to whether such evidence is “necessary”, that term must be relative – it is difficult to conceive of any matter on which it would be literally impossible for a court or tribunal to decide without an expert. In British Airways, “necessary” was contrasted with something “of marginal relevance” (see [63]), and later (at [68]) with something “merely helpful”.

Given the guidance of the Court of Session in Stenhouse that valuation is ultimately “a matter of fact and expert opinion”, expert valuation evidence is clearly closer to being “necessary” than “merely helpful” in a case involving a contentious issue regarding the market value of an asset. In any event, given the conclusions in that case, it is difficult to see how it can properly be said that such evidence is not “reasonably required” to resolve an issue between the parties as to the value of an asset.

Further, even if expert evidence in a valuation matter were only considered to be of “assistance”, it would be necessary to consider the sorts of factors referred to by Warren J in British Airways at [63], as to which:

The value of the claim is for £40.8 million as regards the determination and £12.5 million as regards the NICs decision. In addition, there is interest and HMRC also seek additional amounts in respect of s 222 ITEPA. On any measure, this is a very high value claim. That favours admitting the expert evidence.
Given the size of the claim, which will fall on the appellant, the effect of a judgment either way is of obvious significance. Again, that favours admission.

The appellant has already incurred the costs of instructing Mr Weaver. Indeed, this factor is framed in terms which imply that, at the stage at which the “reasonably required” test is being considered, expert evidence will not have been obtained – “who is to pay for the commissioning”, not “who has paid”. Hence why the test appears to be a permission stage question (not a question to be asked at trial after permission to adduce expert evidence has already been granted and the expert evidence served). Regardless, the appellant has incurred those costs already and has done so on the basis of the tribunal’s permission, to which HMRC consented and after HMRC had been notified in May 2022 that the appellant would be relying on valuation expert evidence. These facts also strongly favour admission.

All of those factors strongly suggest the evidence should be admitted. Accordingly, the expert evidence in this case is far closer to the “necessary” end of the spectrum as opposed to merely “helpful”, but even if it were the latter, the factors highlighted in British Airways overwhelmingly favour the conclusion that Mr Weaver’s evidence is “reasonably required” in the context of this appeal.

Moreover, HMRC do not adequately address the relevant principles. It is notable that HMRC do not address Warren J’s test in British Airways. Instead, HMRC cite arguments none of which properly address the question of whether Mr Weaver’s evidence is “reasonably required” to resolve the proceedings:

They are something of a variety, many of them newly raised, and many seemingly about the principles of valuation. They do not consider the “ultimate question” – what is the “price” for the purposes of s 272 TCGA? That is the issue on which the evidence is called and it is a question of fact.
As regards the contention that the tribunal must decide between two competing analyses of the transaction:
HMRC pose that binary choice but do not provide the tribunal with any basis for, or assistance in, choosing.

The statutory question is actually whether the shares were disposed of for more than their market value as at the disposal date. That involves a question of ascertaining their value as at the disposal date, and that is a question of fact and expert opinion, according to the case law cited above.
As regards HMRC’s comparison of the valuation standards relied on by Mr Weaver with some of the case law:
That involves an assessment of the IVS, which is the preserve of Mr Weaver rather than HMRC.
Mr Weaver cites and applies that IVS guidance, and only that guidance – he does not refer to the case law to which HMRC refer. Nor do those valuation standards refer to any case law.
It seems odd that HMRC essentially criticise Mr Weaver for applying guidance which contain principles which are consistent with the law.
The appellant plainly does rely on the expert evidence of Mr Weaver.

HMRC seek to contrast Grays Timber with other cases on market value, and assert that expert evidence was not reasonably required in that case. However, that proposition is not supported by the judgment: as far as the appellant can tell, there was no discussion of expert evidence, nor any indication that either side sought to rely on expert evidence.

Further, as HMRC’s own Shares and Asset Valuation Manual at SVM113030 says: “it is misleading to think that the decided cases necessarily provide firm pointers for the selection of valuation techniques or data.”
None of the cases referred to by HMRC considers the question of whether expert evidence is reasonably required.
The appellant submitted that HMRC’s second ground has no merit or foundation:

It is, in fact, the correct approach to take for Mr Weaver to rely on the assumptions he has made as regards the facts (see De Sena at [150]). He has not, as HMRC assert, made his own findings of fact.

As Jacob LJ held in esure (cited in Singleton): “It is, of course, permissible for an expert to opine on the ultimate question if it is one of fact, not law”. As the authorities cited show, questions of the value of an asset are questions of fact and opinion.

Mr Weaver has not made his own findings of fact which involve him descending into the arena. In short, he has applied a valuation technique by reference to the facts with which he was provided - he has analysed those facts, which it would have been remiss of him not to have done - and he has sought to apply the valuation principles in the Guidelines to arrive at his opinion. That is a perfectly proper thing for him to have done. If HMRC wished to challenge his understanding of the facts, they have had the opportunity to do so in cross-examination.

That the evidence in the report is “incomplete and untested in cross-examination” is how expert evidence works, given it is necessarily produced before cross-examination. In any event, Mr Weaver has now given evidence, the tribunal has received his opinion after that cross-examination has happened and, therefore, in the light of all of the evidence.

IVS 104 does not mention any case law and does not, as HMRC allege, distil the relevant legal principles that the tribunal is bound to apply; it is consistent with that case law, but that is a different matter. Mr Weaver’s role as a valuer is to apply the valuation guidance that, in his opinion, is applicable to the case.

There is no clear basis for HMRC’s assertion that the valuer ought to base their assessment on “a range of factors” such as cashflow and price-earnings ratios in order for the report to be one by which the tribunal would potentially have been assisted (as in Netley). In his report, Mr Weaver explains that such approaches are effectively proxies for a comparable market transaction. Simply put, an actual transaction in the market is best evidence of market value and other techniques are only required when such suitable comparable transactions, even with qualifications, are not available. In essence, HMRC appear to have overlooked the fact that Mr Weaver’s approach is a technique that valuers use to arrive at a market value. If they wished to challenge his use of that technique, the correct approach would have been for them to call their own expert witness.

HMRC’s contention that Mr Weaver’s report seeks to “apply the legal principles encapsulated in IVS 104 to the detailed primary facts he has found and the inferences he has drawn from them” proceeds on a false premise: (a) IVS 104 is a valuation standard which contains no legal principles; and (b) Mr Weaver has not “found” any facts, for the reasons already given.

There is no parallel between Mr Weaver’s report and the expert report provided in Hastings. Hastings was concerned with issues of VAT which simply involved applying the law in relation to VAT to the facts. It is obvious why an expert’s report which sought to do that would be trespassing on the function of the tribunal. By contrast, matters of valuation – which involve interpreting and applying valuation standards to the facts of a given case – are not within the expertise of the tribunal. Expert valuers are commonly called to assist the tribunal on valuation matters for this reason.

Valuation is necessarily fact-sensitive. It would be remiss of him if Mr Weaver gave a view without assessing the facts and circumstances surrounding the transaction against what he sees as the relevant valuation standards or the basic definition of market value that is in issue. If Mr Weaver had not identified the statutory framework, within which he was opining, then no doubt HMRC would criticise him for that. Further, merely referring to legislation does not render an expert report inadmissible (see Singleton at [18] and [91], citing Deloitte). Mr Weaver has applied valuation guidelines relating to a particular valuation technique to the facts that he was provided with. That is entirely legitimate and perfectly orthodox.

p.span: Conclusion

blockContainer.p: We have concluded that Mr Weaver’s evidence is admissible in these proceedings:

The market value test involves a mixed question of law and fact. The legislation sets out the applicable definition of “market value” and prescribes certain assumptions to be made in performing the valuation and that test and those assumptions have been the subject of much comment in the courts as to how they are to be interpreted and applied.

We accept that, as the appellant submitted, (a) the statutory rule and the guidance from the case law on how it is to be interpreted and applied set the parameters for the factual question of what the market value or “price” is, (b) valuation is a recognised and established field of expertise, and (c) accordingly, in principle, the view of an expert on how the market test would be applied in practice, under applicable valuation principles and guidelines, which accord with and reflect the market value test, depending on the circumstances under consideration, may be of assistance to the tribunal in resolving that question.

As reflects their submissions on the correct approach to the market value test, the appellant submitted that Mr Weaver correctly considered the characteristics and reliability of the actual transaction and, having tested that, used it as a benchmark for the hypothetical transaction on the basis that it does not matter that the relevant shareholders were not actual buyers, as the nature of the exercise is to ascertain whether the actual transactions had the characteristics of a transaction between a “willing buyer” and a “willing seller”. For all the reasons set out in the decision, our view, however, is that such an approach is not permitted according to the approach taken to the correct interpretation of the market value test set out in the caselaw; the legal principles set out by the courts, as derived from their interpretation of the statutory provisions, do not permit such an approach (see [93] to [136] and [253] to [257] of the decision). As Mr Weaver’s evidence is underpinned by that incorrect approach, we derive no assistance from it.

We consider that Mr Weaver’s evidence is nevertheless admissible on the basis that (a) if, contrary to our view, the appellant’s approach to the application of the market value test is correct as a matter of law, it follows that his evidence would be of assistance and would reasonably be required, (b) on that approach, in his evidence, Mr Weaver did not usurp the function of the tribunal; he gave his opinion on how in practice the shares would be valued under the principles in the IVS/Guidelines on the basis of factual assumptions, his understanding of which was tested in cross-examination (albeit that we do not agree that his assumptions reflect a correct understanding of the evidence/facts (see [10] and [30] in this appendix and Part C of the decision, in particular, [130] to [136] and [253] to [257])), and (c) it would be contrary to justice and fairness to deny the appellant the ability to rely on Mr Weaver’s evidence in these proceedings, bearing in mind that there may be an appeal against this decision. Contrary to HMRC’s suggestion, Mr Weaver’s evidence plainly formed a central part of the appellant’s arguments on the market value issue. As set out by the appellant, HMRC raised no objection to the production of expert evidence for a prolonged period during these proceedings and only made an application to the tribunal for it to be excluded during the course of the hearing.

Finally, even if, contrary to our view, Mr Weaver’s evidence were to be taken to be of relevance, we do not accept that, as the appellant submitted, his evidence should be accepted in full, on the basis that the explanations he gave under cross-examination are cogent, rational and in accordance with the Guidelines. In addition to the points already made above in this appendix and in the decision (see Part C, in particular, [130] to [136] and [253] to [257]), we note the following:

The appellant submitted that Mr Weaver’s clear evidence was that Mr Wells was a “willing seller” and that Prism was not “overeager”. However, in our view, Mr Weaver could not adequately explain these concepts and hence why Mr Wells and Prism are to be taken as willing and not overeager respectively. We note that, on his own evidence, Mr Wells was only prepared to sell if there was a “spectacular offer” and that he was “reluctant” accords with Mr Maynard’s evidence also. Mr Jones submitted that the description of Mr Wells as a “reluctant seller”, as HMRC did, is not a concept found anywhere in the Guidelines. However, HMRC used this term, in effect, only as what is meant by unwilling as the opposite of “willing”. Mr Nawbatt submitted that, on the ordinary meaning of the term (by reference to the definition in the Oxford English dictionary), a person is “willing” if he is disposed to consent or comply, ready to do something, specified or desiring to do a particular thing or, not inclined, willing or ready, averse, reluctant or loath. We accept that, on the evidence, Mr Wells was a reluctant or unwilling seller in that sense.

It is not at all clear whether and to what extent Mr Weaver has taken into account the various special terms and/or elements of value which were only available to the particular sellers and so must be excluded from an assessment of the hypothetical sale. He mostly accepted that was the case in his oral evidence, but these factors were mentioned in his report and he did not have adequate explanations as to why that was.

Mr Maynard accepted that, as part of the agreement regarding the allocation or division of the sale proceeds, he and Mr Wells agreed to discontinue the proceedings with Prism. It is for the appellant to show that the allocation did not reflect value attributable to compromising those proceedings. Yet Mr Weaver did not take that into account in his report. Mr Jones submitted that Mr Weaver said as a matter of fact that he had not seen any evidence of the attribution of any value to those proceedings and there were no proceedings in relation to Bond, and yet Bond and Prism received the same amount per share (leaving aside the debt mechanism). However, in our view, as HMRC submitted, this does not demonstrate that no value was attributable to the legal proceedings against Prism. Mr Maynard’s evidence was that Bond followed Prism.

Mr Weaver was not clear about how he viewed the fact that part of the price received by Mr Wells and Mr Maynard for their shares represented a reward for the work which Mr Wells and Mr Maynard had done for the appellant as shown in the correspondence.

It is also unclear how he factored in or discounted the fact that in the discussions both with Prism and with the five other majority shareholders, Mr Wells and Mr Maynard sought to justify the difference in price per share on the basis of the personal warranties that they would be giving.
